records.found: An unreviewed preprint dated 2026-11-04 tested five measures of biological age (built from routine blood tests, a frailty index and telomere length, not from the marks on DNA) in 9,617 Swedish twins and 314,064 UK Biobank people, and found they added a little to the prediction of death beyond age and the usual risk factors. No regulator's clearance and no health system's published routine use of a clock turned up in the window.

findings.what: Preprint (Research Square, not peer reviewed), Mostafaei, Hägg and colleagues: 'Biological aging measures for all-cause mortality prediction in two population-based cohorts'. records.found: The full results of the ZEUS trial of ziltivekimab, which the record holds only as a company announcement, were published in the New England Journal of Medicine on 2026-11-07 and presented at the American Heart Association meeting in Chicago: in 6,376 people the drug cut an inflammation marker by 64 per cent and made no difference to heart attacks, strokes or cardiovascular deaths (17.6 against 17.7 per cent; hazard ratio 0.99, 95 per cent range 0.88 to 1.11), with more serious infections (20.4 against 17.9 per cent) and more serious blood clots in the veins (1.6 against 0.6 per cent). This weighs against the wide-use estimate, because the largest test of a drug acting on inflammation alone is now a peer-reviewed null result with a safety cost, and the investigators' own press release calls colchicine approved but underused; it does not touch colchicine's own trials, so the weight is modest. For the author: the records do not hold that two more ziltivekimab trials in heart failure (HERMES and ATHENA) were stopped early for lack of effect, reported 2026-09-07.

findings.what: Ridker and colleagues, New England Journal of Medicine, 'Interleukin-6 Inhibition with Ziltivekimab for Atherosclerotic Disease' (ZEUS). The journal page refused the fetch; the title, date and authors were confirmed in Crossref's record of the DOI, and the figures below come from three reports opened the same day.

Healio report of the presentation: 6,376 adults with artery disease, chronic kidney disease and raised inflammation; main measure 17.6 per cent on the drug against 17.7 per cent on placebo, hazard ratio 0.99 (0.88 to 1.11), P = .84, median follow-up 33 months; the inflammation marker hsCRP down 64 per cent; serious infections 20.4 against 17.9 per cent. Published in the journal at the same time.

HCPLive report: 561 of 3,184 against 565 of 3,192 events; deaths from any cause 16.9 against 17.0 per cent; serious blood clots in the veins 1.6 against 0.6 per cent, a difference the investigators could only partly explain.

Mass General Brigham press release: the lead investigator says inflammation still causes heart disease, suggests the people enrolled were too far gone or the target too far downstream, points to drugs against the NLRP3 switch upstream, and says low-dose colchicine is approved but underused.

Outside the window and not in the records: Pharmaphorum reports that Novo Nordisk stopped the HERMES and ATHENA heart-failure trials of ziltivekimab after an interim look showed they were unlikely to succeed (first reported by Endpoints; no company release cited). The registry lists HERMES (NCT05636176) as terminated, last updated 2026-10-01. The record's source file still says two further trials read out in the first half of 2027; only ARTEMIS, after a heart attack, remains. Two of the reports of 2026-11-07 still describe HERMES as under way.

Baldwin and colleagues, Cardiovascular Research: placebo-controlled trial of colchicine 0.6 mg a day for 24 weeks in 111 people with chronic coronary disease; it did not reduce inflammation in the wall of the aorta on a scan, its main measure (P = 0.38), while one blood marker of inflammation fell and blood pressure rose less. Abstract read.

Jaiswal and colleagues, American Journal of Cardiovascular Drugs: pooled analysis of nine trials (2,005 people) of colchicine around heart surgery; less irregular heartbeat after surgery, no difference in deaths or strokes. Abstract read.

Registry: new colchicine trials listed in the window, none with results: TARGET-CHD (NCT07920133, colchicine guided by an inflammation marker after a stent, not yet recruiting), a platform trial (NCT07892976) and a kidney-disease pilot (NCT07654231). Listing only.

Registry entry NCT07783802 updated: Eli Lilly's phase 2 trial of clazakizumab, another antibody against interleukin-6, in 120 adults with raised inflammation and heart risk, recruiting; main measure is the inflammation marker at 12 weeks.
Registry entry NCT06263244 (SPIDER, Amsterdam) updated to completed on 2026-10-30: 40 people, ziltivekimab against placebo, artery-wall inflammation on a scan; no results posted.

Donors were healthy, not stated to be young, and the model is induced ageing, not old animals; the authors did not check that the microbes took. Abstract read.

Preprint (Preprints.org), Wu and colleagues: 18 people aged 60 to 80 with Alzheimer's disease given microbe-transfer capsules three times, no control group; thinking scores were higher after the third dose. Uncontrolled and unreviewed, so it cannot meet the first-human test. Abstract read.

Registry entry NCT07462767 updated: Louisiana State University trial of a probiotic bacterium and blueberry extract on worn-out immune cells in 160 people with HIV who drink alcohol; recruiting. A supplement, not a microbe transfer.

unmatched.what: Ryan and colleagues, GeroScience: in 18,581 people aged 65 and over in a placebo-controlled trial, daily low-dose aspirin did not slow decline on a four-part score of function over five years, and decline was slightly faster in women on aspirin; the score tracked DNA-mark clocks. An analysis decided after the trial.
unmatched.why_it_matters: A large negative reading for the idea that damping inflammation preserves function in old age; aspirin is not an inflammation-only drug, so it fits no entry in this packet.
